name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Weeping Beech Park

location.address: Margaret I. Carman Green (Weeping Beech Park), 37th Ave, Flushing

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Flushing-Main St station (7 train, LIRR), about 0.7 km on foot
verify_notes: Source: NYC Parks Great Trees entry id=47 (fetched live 2026-11-02, carries lat/lon and a Tree Map ID, the Parks forestry inventory's individual-tree id). Diameter 59 in -> girth_cm 471 (pi x diameter). One official register: counts as enough; Parks entry: mid-park near the public restroom; began life in the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, whose grounds ran through this area; canopy spread 59 ft. Register 1985 nomination, still on the 2024 relaunched list with Tree Map ID 5063634. Sits beside nyc_028 (Weeping Beech Park, pin 40.7636,-73.8242), about 50 m away: a two-tree stop. Register diameter 59 in is the 1985 measurement. iNaturalist observation 2026-06-16 within radius.
story:
This cedar started out as stock in a nursery that once covered this corner of Flushing. The parks department's Great Trees entry says it began life in the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, whose grounds ran through the area, and the park around it takes its name from another tree, a weeping beech.

The cedar is the less famous neighbour and the stranger shape. The register gives it a height of only 12.7 metres but a crown spreading 59 feet, about 18 metres, so it is far wider than it is tall, the flat-topped, layered build of a cedar of Lebanon that has had room to spread. Its trunk measured 59 inches across, about 4.7 metres round, when the city named it a Great Tree in 1985. That figure is four decades old, and the tree has kept the title through the 2024 revision of the list.

Cedar of Lebanon comes from the mountains of the eastern Mediterranean, the tree of the Lebanese flag. That one should have reached Queens through a nineteenth-century nursery catalogue is very much the Parsons story, a family that sold exotic trees to the gardens of a growing country.

It stands in the middle of the park, near the public restroom, about 50 metres from the weeping beech, so the two make one stop. The park is free and open daily. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its flat, layered crown, about 18 metres across on a tree under 13 metres tall. It stands in the middle of the park near the public restroom, about 50 metres from the weeping beech.

name: The Ginkgo of John Golden Park

location.address: John Golden Park (Crocheron Park area), Bayside

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Bayside station (LIRR, Port Washington branch), about 1.3 km on foot
story:
Boss Tweed is said to have hidden from the law near this ginkgo. NYC Parks links the tree to William M. Tweed, who escaped from Ludlow Street Jail and, by the account on its Great Trees entry, lay low at the Crocheron family house that once stood on this ground. The city later bought the property, and the land is now John Golden Park. The Tweed story is Parks' telling and we have found it nowhere else, so treat it as local lore rather than a court record.

The tree itself needs no legend. It is about 25 metres tall, with a trunk 37 inches across, close to three metres round, and a crown about 33 feet wide. It went on the Great Trees list in the city's first survey, in 1985, and an iNaturalist record from July 2026 shows it still standing. Nobody has published when it was planted, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

It stands behind the baseball fields, near the public restroom, in a free park in Bayside that is open every day. Bayside station on the Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington branch is about 1.3 kilometres away on foot. Come in November, when a ginkgo turns butter yellow.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves and a trunk close to three metres round. It stands behind the baseball fields near the public restroom in John Golden Park, Bayside.

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn butter yellow

name: The Swamp White Oak of Bowne Park

location.address: Bowne Park, between the northwest entrance and the pond, Flushing

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Flushing-Main St (7 train, LIRR), about 2.3 km; local bus from Main St
story:
NYC Parks did not hedge on this one. When the swamp white oak in Bowne Park joined the Great Trees list in 2024, the citation called it an exceptionally large tree for its kind and the most impressive tree in the park. The trunk is 50 inches across, close to four metres round, a serious waistline for an oak named after wet ground and here growing in a neighbourhood park in Queens.

The 2024 listing came out of the city's Great Tree Search, nearly four decades after the first list of 1985, and it put this oak among the newest names on the roll. Parks gives its Tree Map number, 5085084, so you can find the same trunk in the city's forestry inventory, and an iNaturalist record from August 2025 shows it still standing.

What nobody has published is its age. Nothing we have read dates this tree, and we will not guess from the size of the trunk. If you know when it went in, or what the ground looked like before the park, tell us.

It stands between the northwest entrance and the pond, in a free park open daily. Flushing-Main Street, the end of the 7 train and a Long Island Rail Road stop, is about 2.3 kilometres away, with local buses from Main Street.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 50 inches across, close to four metres round. It stands between the northwest entrance and the pond in Bowne Park, Flushing.

name: The Fused Basswood of Fort Totten

location.address: Fort Totten Park, Underhill Rd and Officers Dr, Bayside

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park (Fort Totten Park); the former army post is open to walkers
transport: Bayside station (LIRR) about 2.7 km; local bus to Fort Totten
story: Measured across the trunk, this basswood at Fort Totten comes out at 99 inches, close to the width of a single garage door. That number needs an asterisk, and NYC Parks gives it one. The tree is not one stem but several that grew side by side and fused together long ago, so the 99 inches is the width of a fused mass rather than a single trunk. Round, that works out at about 7.9 metres of wood at chest height, and a shape you will not mistake for anything else in the park. It is also a reminder that the biggest number on a list is not always the oldest tree. A fused basswood can carry a girth that a single trunk of the same age never would, and the honest reading of this one is a big, strange, many-stemmed tree of unknown age. Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, when the city relaunched its roll of remarkable trees. It stands at the corner of Underhill Road and Officers Drive, on the grounds of Fort Totten in Bayside, a former army post that is now a public park open to walkers. Somebody has seen it recently. An iNaturalist record from July 2025 sits near the Parks point. Nobody has recorded when the stems first came up or when they joined. If you know the tree's history, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, several stems fused into one mass about 99 inches across. It stands at the corner of Underhill Road and Officers Drive in Fort Totten Park.

name: The Willow Oak of Steinway Street

location.address: 23-24 Steinway Street, Astoria

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: Astoria Blvd station (N, W), about 0.8 km on foot
story:
This oak waves at trains. That is NYC Parks' own phrase for the willow oak outside 23-24 Steinway Street, whose branches reach toward the trains crossing the Hell Gate Bridge, and it is a fair description of a street tree that has grown far bigger than the sidewalk it was given.

The trunk is 42 inches across, about 3.4 metres round. Parks called it extremely large when it joined the Great Trees list in 2024, and it earned that on what Parks describes as a busy commercial and residential stretch of Astoria. Most of the city's great trees have a park around them. This one has a sidewalk and the traffic of Steinway Street.

A willow oak is easy to mistake for something else. The leaves are narrow and pointed, more like a willow's than an oak's, and only the acorns give it away. Nobody has published when this one was planted, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

An iNaturalist record from September 2026 shows it standing. It is on the public sidewalk, so you can see it at any hour. The Astoria Boulevard station on the N and W lines is about 800 metres away on foot.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the narrow, willow-like leaves on a trunk about 3.4 metres round. It stands on the sidewalk outside 23-24 Steinway Street, Astoria.

name: The River Birch of Corporal Kennedy Street

location.address: 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street, Bayside

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: Bayside station (LIRR), about 0.5 km on foot
story:
A river birch this size is unusual anywhere, and NYC Parks found one growing out of a Bayside sidewalk. The tree outside 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street has several stems that together measure 57 inches across, about 4.5 metres round, and a canopy that arches clear over the street. Parks put it on the Great Trees list in 2024 and named exactly that as the reason, a very large multi-stemmed river birch, uncommon at this size and more uncommon still as a street tree.

The number needs one caution. A multi-stemmed tree is measured across its stems, so 57 inches is the mass of several trunks rising from one base, not a single column of wood. That is also what you see standing under it, a cluster rather than a pillar.

Nobody has published its age. The latest sighting we found is an iNaturalist record from August 2024, recent enough to trust but not as fresh as we would like. If you pass it and it is still there, or if you know when it was planted, tell us.

It stands on the public sidewalk, so it can be seen at any time. Bayside station on the Long Island Rail Road is about 500 metres away on foot, and the ginkgo of John Golden Park, another Great Tree, is about a kilometre to the north.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by several stems rising from one base, together 57 inches across, under a canopy that arches across the street. It stands on the sidewalk outside 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street, Bayside.

name: The London Plane of Alice Austen Park

location.address: Alice Austen Park, meadow south of the Alice Austen House, Rosebank

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Alice Austen Park open daily; the house museum has separate hours and a suggested donation
transport: Staten Island Railway Clifton station, about 0.6 km; or S51/S78 bus on Bay St (check route)
story: Lightning has hit this plane tree and left its mark, and it is still standing in the meadow south of the Alice Austen House. NYC Parks records the scar on its Great Trees entry, along with the detail that the tree is alive in spite of it. Parks also gives it a starting point. It is believed to have been growing here around 1840, when John Austen, Alice Austen's grandfather, bought the house and set about expanding it. Believed is Parks' word, with no planting record behind it, so read 1840 as a family-era tradition rather than a date. If it holds, the tree is more than 185 years old. The measurements are from the 1985 survey that first put it on the list. The trunk was 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, with a crown spreading almost 60 feet over the meadow, though at about 19 metres tall it is broad rather than towering. An iNaturalist record from July 2026 places it alive. Alice Austen Park is open daily and free. The house museum has its own hours and asks a suggested donation, but the tree stands outside it, in the meadow south of the house in Rosebank, on the Staten Island shore. Von Briesen Park, with its own Great Tree, is close by along the same shore. If you know more about when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide crown, spreading almost 60 feet on a trunk 54 inches across, and its lightning scar. It stands in the meadow south of the Alice Austen House in Alice Austen Park, Rosebank.

name: The Princess Tree of Snug Harbor

location.address: Snug Harbor Cultural Center, west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse, Chapel Road, 1000 Richmond Terrace (Parks lists 914)

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Grounds free, open dawn to dusk seven days a week (Snug Harbor official material via search; some buildings and the Chinese Scholar's Garden take a small fee)
transport: Staten Island Ferry to St George, then S40 bus to Snug Harbor (route unchecked this pass)
story: When NYC Parks measured this tree for its first Great Trees list in 1985, the trunk came out at 65 inches across, about 5.2 metres round. It is a royal paulownia, the tree also called princess tree or empress tree, and it stands on the grounds of Snug Harbor on Staten Island, on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse off Chapel Road. Parks notes two things that make it easy to pick out. The leaves can grow up to a foot across, big enough to look like a mistake, and in spring the tree carries purple trumpet-shaped flowers. Parks put its height at about 20 metres, so the trunk is the surprise rather than the crown. Snug Harbor is a cultural centre now, and its grounds are free to walk, open from dawn to dusk every day; a few buildings and the Chinese Scholar's Garden charge a small fee, but the paulownia is outside them. One honest caveat about the address. Parks lists the tree at 914 Richmond Terrace and Snug Harbor gives its own address as 1000, but both point to the same campus, and the playhouse is the landmark that matters. The measurements are forty years old. If you have seen it lately or know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, up to a foot across, and in spring by purple trumpet flowers. It stands on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse at Snug Harbor, off Chapel Road.

name: The Willow Oak of Clove Lake

location.address: Clove Lakes Park, shore of Clove Lake, 150 ft north of Victory Blvd near the basketball courts

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Bus on Victory Blvd from St George; about 3 km from the SIR
story:
NYC Parks listed this tree as half of a pair. On the shore of Clove Lake, about 150 feet north of Victory Boulevard, two willow oaks share a single entry on the Great Trees list, which they have held since the city's first survey in 1985. The entry gives one set of measurements for the pair, a trunk 43 inches across, about 3.4 metres round, close to 26 metres of height and a crown spreading some 43 feet at the water's edge.

The name tells you what to look for. A willow oak has narrow leaves that read as willow from a distance, which is a neat trick for a tree standing beside a lake where you would expect real willows. Up close the acorns settle it.

Nobody has published when the pair went in, so the age stays open. If you know, tell us. An iNaturalist record from September 2026 shows them still standing.

Clove Lakes Park is free and open daily, and the walk is the reason to come. The Clove Lakes Colossus, a tulip tree and Staten Island's tallest, stands about 1.3 kilometres away at the north end of the same park, so the two make one lake walk. The oaks are by the basketball courts near Victory Boulevard, reached by bus from St George.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the narrow, willow-like leaves on two big oaks side by side at the water. It stands on the Clove Lake shore, about 150 feet north of Victory Boulevard near the basketball courts.

name: The Cedar of Lebanon of the Olmsted-Beil House

location.address: Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, Great Kills area

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free public park around the house; Parks lists it as a city park
transport: Eltingville SIR station about 1.2 km; S55/S59 buses on Hylan Blvd (unchecked)
story: This cedar of Lebanon grows on the farm where Frederick Law Olmsted worked the land for seven years before he designed Central Park. Olmsted farmed here, on Staten Island, from 1848 to 1855, and NYC Parks counts the cedar as one of the trees still remaining from that farm. Parks stops short of saying who planted it or when, so we do too. It is tempting to credit Olmsted with it, and the honest answer is that nobody has. What Parks does give is a location so exact you could use it as directions. The tree stands 35 feet off the left front corner of the house and three feet off the driveway. It measures 46 inches across the trunk, about 3.7 metres round, stands about 82 feet tall and spreads its crown about 40 feet. It has been on the Great Trees list since 1985, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees, and an iNaturalist record from May 2024 places it alive. A black walnut that Parks says Olmsted planted stands about 25 metres away, so see both. The park around the house is free. Nobody has dated the cedar. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the position, 35 feet off the left front corner of the house and three feet off the driveway. It stands at Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, about 25 metres from the black walnut.

name: The Black Walnut Olmsted Planted

location.address: Olmsted-Beil House Park, east of the house, 4515 Hylan Boulevard

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free public park around the house
transport: Eltingville SIR station about 1.2 km (unchecked bus routes)
story: Before Frederick Law Olmsted designed Central Park, he was a farmer on Staten Island, and NYC Parks says he planted this black walnut himself. Olmsted lived in the house on Hylan Boulevard from 1848 to 1855, and Parks, naming the tree a Great Tree in 2024, credits him with this one and says many of the trees on the property went in around 1850. That makes it, if Parks is right, a tree put in the ground by the man who went on to design Central Park. Take it as Parks' claim. It is the only source we have, and we have found no letter or planting record to back it, so we state it as theirs rather than as settled fact. The tree itself makes a quieter case. Its trunk measures 52 inches across, about 4.2 metres round, which is a big black walnut by any measure. It stands east of the house, about 25 metres from a cedar of Lebanon that Parks also counts among the trees left from Olmsted's farm, so the two make a single stop. The house sits in Olmsted-Beil House Park, a free public park in the Great Kills area. Nobody has measured its age directly. If you know more about what Olmsted planted here, or have seen his own notes on it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 52 inches across, the big walnut on the east side of the house. It stands in Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, about 25 metres from the cedar of Lebanon.

name: The American Sycamore of Conference House Park

location.address: Conference House Park, behind the Conference House, Tottenville

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Conference House Park free, open daily; the house museum charges a small fee in season
transport: Tottenville SIR station about 1.1 km on foot
story: The house in front of this sycamore hosted a peace conference in 1776. It is the Conference House in Tottenville, on Staten Island, and NYC Parks puts this American sycamore directly behind it. Do not read that as a witness claim. Parks gives no planting date, and nothing says the tree was here for the conference. The house is the history and the tree is its neighbour today. What the register does give is size. When the tree was first listed as a Great Tree in 1985, it measured 65 inches across the trunk, about 5.2 metres round, and 89 feet tall, with a crown spreading 55 feet. Those are the figures of a tree that has had plenty of room, out on open parkland at the back of a historic house rather than on a crowded street. The tree is still there. An iNaturalist record from September 2026 sits near the Parks point, and the city keeps it in its forestry inventory. Conference House Park is free and open daily; the house museum charges a small fee in season, but the sycamore stands outside it on public parkland. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 65 inches across, and its crown spreading about 55 feet. It stands directly behind the Conference House in Conference House Park, Tottenville.

name: The Pagoda Tree of Von Briesen Park

location.address: Von Briesen Park, southern end where the path curves east-west, Rosebank

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Clifton SIR station about 0.9 km; 1.3 km from nyc_076 (a short walk from Alice Austen Park)
story:
The man who founded the Legal Aid Society may have known this tree. NYC Parks believes the Japanese pagoda tree at the southern end of Von Briesen Park was part of the original estate of Arthur Von Briesen, whose heirs gave the land to the city in 1945. Believed is Parks' word, and no planting record has surfaced to firm it up, so read the estate link as likely rather than proven.

What is not in doubt is its size. The trunk is 48 inches across, about 3.8 metres round, and Parks called it unusually large for its species when it named the tree a Great Tree in 2024. An iNaturalist record from August 2026 shows it still standing.

It also blooms late, which is its best trick. In late summer, when most trees have long finished, it hangs out pendant sprays of flowers. Nobody has published its age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

Find it where the path curves from east to west at the south end of the park, which is free and open daily. Clifton station on the Staten Island Railway is about 900 metres away, and the plane tree of Alice Austen Park is about 1.3 kilometres along the same shore, so the two make one walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad trunk, about 3.8 metres round, and in late summer its hanging sprays of flowers. It stands where the path curves east to west at the south end of Von Briesen Park.

best_time.label: August, when it hangs out pendant sprays of flowers long after other trees have finished

name: The White Pine of Blue Heron Park

location.address: Blue Heron Park Preserve, just southeast of the Blue Heron Nature Center

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free public park preserve, open daily
transport: Annadale SIR station, about 1 km (unchecked)
story:
This is the last of its kind in Blue Heron Park. NYC Parks says the eastern white pine just southeast of the Blue Heron Nature Center is the only white pine of this size left in the preserve, and it chose the tree for the Great Trees list in 2024 for its age rather than its bulk.

That choice shows in the numbers. The trunk is 27 inches across, about 2.2 metres round, slim beside the oaks and planes on the rest of the city's list. The height is another matter. Parks gives it about 90 feet, close to 27 metres, and a white pine puts that height into one straight stem, so this tree reads as a mast rather than a crown.

Parks does not say how old it is, only that age was the reason it was picked, and nobody else has published a figure. We will not invent one from the trunk. If you know its story, or when the pines around it went, tell us.

Blue Heron Park Preserve is free and open daily, in Annadale on the South Shore of Staten Island. Start at the nature center and look southeast. The Annadale station on the Staten Island Railway is roughly a kilometre away. An iNaturalist record from October 2026 shows the pine still standing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a single straight trunk about 90 feet tall, the only white pine that size in the preserve. It stands just southeast of the Blue Heron Nature Center in Blue Heron Park Preserve.

name: The Catalpa of Historic Richmond Town

location.address: Historic Richmond Town, behind the tin shop, 441 Clarke Avenue (Parks lists LaTourette Park)

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Ticketed village (open Wednesday to Sunday per search results; check historicrichmondtown.org for hours and price)
transport: Bus from St George (S74 to Richmond Rd, unchecked); no rail
story:
Behind a tin shop in New York City's only historic village restoration stands a catalpa with a trunk 47 inches across. That is about 3.75 metres round, and it is why NYC Parks named this tree to the Great Trees list in 2024. The citation is short. Parks chose it for its large size and left the rest to the setting.

The setting is Historic Richmond Town, founded in 1939 by the Staten Island Historical Society. It now covers more than 100 acres and over two dozen buildings dating from the 17th century to the 20th, so the tree keeps company with buildings from four centuries of Staten Island life. Parks files it under neighbouring LaTourette Park, but it is the village you walk through to reach it.

Parks names only the genus, catalpa, and not the species. If you can tell from the leaves or the long seed pods, tell us. Nobody has published its age either, and the village's founding date says nothing about when the tree went in.

Entry to the village needs a ticket, and by most accounts it opens from Wednesday to Sunday, so check historicrichmondtown.org for hours and prices before you go. The address is 441 Clarke Avenue, with buses from St George.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the catalpa's big heart-shaped leaves on a trunk about 3.75 metres round. It stands at the back of the tin shop inside Historic Richmond Town, 441 Clarke Avenue.

name: The Davis Hybrid Oak of Stuyvesant Place

location.address: Stuyvesant Place near St. George Park, St. George

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: St. George station (SIR, Staten Island Ferry terminal), about 0.3 km on foot
story: This sidewalk oak is a cross between two species, and it grows a short walk from the Staten Island Ferry. NYC Parks names it Quercus x filialis, a hybrid of black oak and willow oak, first described by the Staten Island naturalist William T. Davis from Tottenville, at the island's southern tip. Parks offers it as a picture of what Staten Island is botanically, a place where the ranges of southern and northern oaks overlap. In 2024 the city made this one a Great Tree. It does not stand in a botanical garden or behind a gate. It grows on Stuyvesant Place near St. George Park, about 300 metres from the ferry terminal, so anyone already crossing the harbour can reach it in five minutes on foot. Its trunk is 43 inches across, a little over three metres round. One oddity in the paperwork. The Parks page heads the entry swamp white oak, which looks like a slip, since the botanical name on the same page describes the black and willow hybrid. The Latin is the one to trust. Nobody has published when it was planted, and the register gives no age, so that stays an open question. If you know this tree's year, or remember the block before it, tell us. Step off the ferry and, a few blocks on, you have found a small botanical argument standing on the pavement, in full view and free.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, a little over three metres round, on a street tree on Stuyvesant Place. It stands on the sidewalk near St. George Park, about 300 metres from the ferry terminal.

name: The American Elm of Sunset Park

location.address: Sunset Park, top of the hill in the central lawn

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: 36 St station (D, N, R), about 0.9 km on foot
story:
This elm was the face of the hunt before it was a winner. When NYC Parks ran its Great Tree Search in 2023, asking New Yorkers to put forward the city's best trees, the advertising photo was the silhouette of this American elm on the hill in Sunset Park. A year later Parks put it on the Great Trees list itself.

It earned the picture on shape more than size. The trunk is 38 inches across, about three metres round, respectable rather than record-breaking. What Parks chose to show was the outline of the tree against the sky at the top of the central lawn, and an American elm's crown is the kind of outline that sells a campaign. The species was hit hard across the Northeast by Dutch elm disease, which makes a healthy one in an open lawn worth the climb.

Nobody has published its age, so we leave it open. If you know when it went in, tell us. An iNaturalist record from September 2025 shows it standing.

Sunset Park is free and open daily, on the Brooklyn slope above the harbour. Walk up to the top of the hill in the central lawn. The 36th Street station on the D, N and R lines is about 900 metres away on foot.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the outline Parks used to advertise its 2023 Great Tree Search, an American elm on the skyline. It stands at the top of the hill in the central lawn of Sunset Park.

name: The Elm of Amersfort Park

location.address: Amersfort Park, near the Avenue J and East 39th Street entrance, Flatlands

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Bus on Avenue J / Flatbush Ave; no close subway (unchecked)
story:
Five feet across is a lot of elm. The American elm near the Avenue J and East 39th Street entrance of Amersfort Park has a trunk 60 inches in diameter, about 4.8 metres round, and NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024. Its citation calls it a tall elm and one of many old-growth trees in Amersfort Park, which says something about this small park in Flatlands. Parks picked one trunk, and named the crowd around it in the same breath.

Nobody has published its age, and a wide trunk alone cannot date a tree, so the age stays open. Old growth is Parks' phrase for the park's trees as a group, not a date for this one. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

One honest caution. The most recent sighting we found is an iNaturalist record from September 2023, which is older than we would like for a tree we send people to. Parks still lists it on its Great Trees map. If you visit and it is standing, or if it is not, tell us so we can keep this page right.

The park is free and open daily. There is no subway close by, so take a bus along Avenue J or Flatbush Avenue and walk in from the Avenue J and East 39th Street corner, where the elm stands.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 60 inches across, about 4.8 metres round. It stands near the Avenue J and East 39th Street entrance of Amersfort Park, Flatlands.

name: The Weeping Willow of Marine Park

location.address: Marine Park, near Gerritsen Ballfields, southeast of Ball Field 3

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Bus only (B3, B41 area; unchecked)
story:
This willow comes with its own seating. NYC Parks, naming it a Great Tree in 2024, noted that it is framed by benches and a path, so the tree had a place to sit under long before it had a title. It stands near the Gerritsen Ballfields, southeast of Ball Field 3, in Marine Park, in southeast Brooklyn.

The trunk is 38 inches across, about three metres round, a real girth for a weeping willow. Parks gives the trunk size and its Tree Map id, 5309024, so this is one tree in the city's forestry inventory you can check against what you see. An iNaturalist record from September 2026 shows it still standing.

What is missing is any date. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is, and we would rather say so than guess from the size of the trunk. If you know, or if you remember the benches going in, tell us.

Marine Park is free and open daily. There is no subway nearby, so come by bus along the B3 or B41 routes and walk to the Gerritsen Ballfields. Look for Ball Field 3, then for the willow southeast of it, with the benches and path around it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hanging curtain of a weeping willow over benches and a path. It stands near the Gerritsen Ballfields, southeast of Ball Field 3, in Marine Park.

name: The Black Oak of Albany Avenue

location.address: 1319 Albany Avenue, East Flatbush

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: Bus on Albany Ave; Utica Av and Nostrand stations are over 1.5 km (unchecked)
story:
This oak was here before the houses. NYC Parks says the black oak outside 1319 Albany Avenue predates the residential development of East Flatbush, and believes it stands where the Paerdegat Woods once grew. The Brooklyn Paper has reported that those woods were cut in the 1940s. If Parks is right, this street tree is not a street tree at all, but a survivor of a forest that the street replaced.

Believes is the word Parks uses, and we keep it. No survey has tied this trunk to the old woods by date, and the age of the tree has never been published. What can be measured is the trunk, 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round, and Parks named it a Great Tree in 2024.

It has a partner. About 240 metres east, outside 1281 Troy Avenue, a second black oak with an even wider trunk carries the same story, and Parks lists the two as the remnants of the same woods. Seeing both takes a few minutes on foot.

Both stand on the public sidewalk, so you can see them at any time. Buses run along Albany Avenue. The nearest subway stations, Utica Avenue and Nostrand Avenue, are more than 1.5 kilometres away. If you know how old these oaks are, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round, on a residential sidewalk. It stands outside 1319 Albany Avenue, East Flatbush; its twin is 240 metres east on Troy Avenue.

name: The Black Oak of Troy Avenue

location.address: 1281 Troy Avenue, East Flatbush

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: Bus on Albany Ave / Clarendon Rd (unchecked)
story:
Fifty-two inches of black oak stand outside 1281 Troy Avenue, and NYC Parks thinks the trunk is older than the block. This is the wider of two black oaks in East Flatbush that Parks named Great Trees in 2024 and believes to be remnants of the Paerdegat Woods, a stretch of woodland the Brooklyn Paper says was cut down in the 1940s. The trunk measures about 4.15 metres round.

The idea is simple enough to picture. When the woods went and the streets were laid out, a few big trees were left standing where the sidewalk now runs. Nobody has published a record showing that happened to this one, so the woods connection stays as Parks frames it, a belief rather than a documented history. The tree's age has never been published either.

Its partner stands about 240 metres west, outside 1319 Albany Avenue, with a trunk of 47 inches. Parks tells the same story for both, and the walk from one to the other takes a few minutes.

The tree is on the public sidewalk and can be seen at any hour. Buses run along Albany Avenue and Clarendon Road. If you know how old it is, or remember the woods, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 52 inches across, about 4.15 metres round, the wider of the two East Flatbush black oaks. It stands outside 1281 Troy Avenue; its twin is 240 metres west on Albany Avenue.

name: The Pawpaw of the Plant Family Collection

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, Plant Family Collection between Daffodil Hill and Oak Circle, 990 Washington Ave

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden (check bbg.org for hours, prices and free times)
transport: Botanic Garden (2, 3, 4, 5) or Prospect Park (B, Q) stations, about 0.4 km
story: Its trunk is only ten inches across, and New York has counted it among its Great Trees since 1985. This is a pawpaw, a member of the custard-apple family, and NYC Parks describes its fruit as edible and banana-like and its leaves as large and umbrella-like. A trunk you could nearly close your hands around sits on the same official roll as the city's giant elms and oaks. It stands in the Plant Family Collection of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, between Daffodil Hill and Oak Circle, about ten metres tall with a crown a little over seven metres wide. The Parks entry gives a planting year of 1923, which makes it roughly a century old. The Parks list page has also carried 1932, and no other source we know of settles it, so treat the century as approximate, give or take a decade. Either date means the tree had already been growing in Brooklyn for half a century or more when the city first drew up its list of Great Trees, and it has stayed on that list for forty years since. Whatever earned it that place, it was not size. Come for a fruit nobody expects in Brooklyn, on a tree that has lasted. Entry to the garden is paid, with free times; check bbg.org before you go. Our pin is approximate, inside the garden, so find the collection first and the tree second.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the large, umbrella-like leaves on a small tree, about ten metres tall with a trunk only ten inches across. It stands in the Plant Family Collection, between Daffodil Hill and Oak Circle.

name: The Chinese Parasol Tree of the Rock Garden

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, south of the Rock Garden

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden (check bbg.org)
transport: Botanic Garden (2, 3, 4, 5) or Prospect Park (B, Q) stations, about 0.5 km
story: This tree arrived in Brooklyn by government post. In 1971 the US National Arboretum sent it to the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, and fourteen years later, in 1985, it was on the city's first list of Great Trees. Fourteen years from arrival to the city's honour roll is fast going. It is a Chinese parasol tree, Firmiana simplex. NYC Parks records a crown about 25 feet across over a trunk only 12.25 inches thick, and a height of about twelve metres. On a tree this slim, the canopy carries the whole effect. Its age is about as well known as any tree's in the garden, since the arrival is on record, so it is a little over half a century old. Nothing older is being claimed for it, and nothing needs to be. It stands just south of the Rock Garden, which puts it in good company. The Great Tree winterberry grows about 25 metres away, and the garden's Caucasian wingnut, another Great Tree, is in the same corner, so three of the city's listed trees can be seen in a few minutes without retracing your steps. Our pin is approximate, since the register gives coordinates inside the garden but no map id for the tree. Entry to the garden is paid, with some free times; check bbg.org before you go.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a broad crown, about 25 feet across, on a slim trunk barely a foot thick. It stands just south of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the Great Tree winterberry.

name: The Winterberry of the Rock Garden

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, south side of the Rock Garden

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden (check bbg.org)
transport: Botanic Garden (2, 3, 4, 5) or Prospect Park (B, Q) stations, about 0.5 km
story: When the city measured this holly in 1985, its trunk was 27.5 inches across, about 2.2 metres round. The tree is a mountain winterberry, Ilex montana, a holly, and it has been one of New York's Great Trees since that first list. NYC Parks records it at about 11.7 metres tall with a crown 28 feet wide. It stands on the south side of the Rock Garden at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden. The Parks entry ties the species to the garden's beginning, noting winterberry among the 12,000 plants the garden advertised when it was founded in 1910. Read that carefully. It says the garden had winterberries from the start. It does not say this is one of them, and no source gives this tree a planting date. So its age is open, and if anyone at the garden knows its history, we would like to hear it. The 1985 measurement is the latest the register gives, so the trunk you see today may well be larger. The tree is still on the city's list forty years on. The register pin sits inside the garden without a map id for the individual tree, so ours is approximate. The Chinese parasol tree, also a Great Tree, stands about 25 metres away, and the garden's Caucasian wingnut is in the same corner. Entry is paid, with some free times; check bbg.org.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a holly grown to tree size, about 11.7 metres tall with a crown 28 feet wide. It stands on the south side of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the Chinese parasol tree.

name: The Pagoda Tree by the Camperdown Elm

location.address: Prospect Park, beside the Camperdown elm south of the Boathouse

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Prospect Park station (B, Q), about 0.3 km on foot
story:
Most people who come to see Brooklyn's famous Camperdown elm walk straight past the bigger tree beside it. This Japanese pagoda tree stands a few steps away, south of the Prospect Park Boathouse, and when NYC Parks named it one of the Great Trees of New York City in 1985 it measured 86 feet tall, about 26 metres, with a crown 62 feet wide. The elm, low and propped on cables, reaches about a quarter of that height.

The trunk is 55 inches across, which works out at about 4.4 metres round, thicker than its famous neighbour's. Parks notes that the species is native to eastern Asia and was once planted at the graves of Japanese scholars. Here it keeps company with rowers and dog walkers instead.

It also keeps its own calendar. Most trees in the park have finished flowering by June. This one waits for late summer, then opens clusters of white flowers when everything around it has gone plain green. An iNaturalist record from October 2026 shows it still standing, four decades after the city first put its name on the list.

Nobody has published when it was planted, and the Parks entry gives no age. If you know, tell us.

The park is free and open daily, and Prospect Park station on the B and Q lines is about 300 metres away. Come for the elm, stay for the tree that towers over it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, far above the low, cabled Camperdown elm beside it, and in late summer by its white flower clusters. It stands a few steps from that elm, south of the Boathouse.

best_time.label: August, when white flower clusters open after most of the park has finished flowering

name: The Multi-Trunk English Elm of the West Drive

location.address: Prospect Park, west drive between the Garfield Entrance and Meadowport Arch

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Grand Army Plaza station (2, 3), about 0.5 km on foot
story: NYC Parks keeps this elm on its Great Trees list partly as a lesson in shape. The native American elm grows in the shape of a vase. This is an English elm, an introduced tree, and it does something else entirely. It rises on several trunks at once, and Parks chose it in 1985 to show the difference. The size is real but needs one caveat. Parks measured it at 74 inches across, about 5.9 metres round, which would make it a giant among elms, but that figure is taken across a mass of several stems rather than one trunk, so do not compare it with a single-stemmed tree. The other numbers need no caveat. It stood 96 feet tall at that survey, about 29 metres, with a crown spreading 66 feet over the West Drive, and it is still there; an iNaturalist record from May 2026 sits near the Parks point. It stands on Prospect Park's West Drive, between the Garfield entrance and Meadowport Arch, on free public parkland open daily. The Camperdown Elm near the Boathouse is in the same park for a second stop. Nobody has dated this one. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its several trunks rising together, unlike the single vase-shaped stem of an American elm. It stands beside Prospect Park's West Drive, between the Garfield entrance and Meadowport Arch.

name: The Elm of Owl's Head Park

location.address: 72nd Street and Ridge Boulevard, near Owl's Head Park, Bay Ridge

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Street tree on the public sidewalk, always viewable
transport: Bus on Ridge Blvd; R train at 77 St about 1 km (unchecked)
story:
Dutch elm disease missed this one. The American elm at 72nd Street and Ridge Boulevard in Bay Ridge escaped the disease that has killed so many American elms, and NYC Parks records that survival on its Great Trees entry. It also records that the neighbourhood picked it. The tree was selected by the community for its remarkable size when the city drew up its first Great Trees list in 1985.

The 1985 survey measured a trunk 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round, and a height of 78 feet, close to 24 metres. Those figures are now four decades old, and an elm that has kept growing since may well be larger, but nobody has published a newer measurement. Nobody has published its age either. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

An iNaturalist record from March 2026 shows it still standing, at a corner beside Owl's Head Park, so a visit can carry on into the park itself.

It is a street tree on the public sidewalk, open to see at any hour. Buses run along Ridge Boulevard, and the R train stops at 77th Street, about a kilometre to the south.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a big American elm, 47 inches across and 78 feet tall when measured in 1985, on a street corner. It stands at 72nd Street and Ridge Boulevard, beside Owl's Head Park, Bay Ridge.

name: The Parrotia of Kissena Park

location.address: Kissena Park, thirty feet south of the public restroom

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Free, public park, open daily
transport: Flushing-Main St (7 train, LIRR), about 2.7 km; local bus
story: A tree native to Iran stands thirty feet south of a public restroom in Queens, and the city lists it among its Great Trees. This is a Persian parrotia, a species NYC Parks calls rare, and it grows in Kissena Park in Flushing, about 17 metres tall with a crown some 44 feet across. Parks presents it as a living record of the trees introduced by the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, and it has been on the city's list of Great Trees since the first one, in 1985. Forty years on that list is a long run for any tree. The trunk is 16 inches across, a little over a metre round, slim beside the giant oaks and elms on the same roll. Look closely at the bark, which Parks describes as brown and flaky, the detail most worth stopping for on a tree whose size will not stop you on its own. Nobody has published a planting date, so we give it no age. If the park's history records when this one went in, or you know more about the Parsons connection, tell us. The directions on the register are refreshingly practical, and they are the best ones we have. Find the restroom and walk thirty feet south. Our pin is approximate, since the register gives no map id for the individual tree. About 90 metres away stands the park's Manchurian linden, another Great Tree, so the two make one short stop.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the brown, flaky bark on a slim trunk about 16 inches across. It stands thirty feet south of the public restroom in Kissena Park, about 90 metres from the Manchurian linden.

name: The Riis Beeches of Maple Grove Cemetery

location.address: Maple Grove Cemetery, by the grave of Elizabeth Riis, Kew Gardens

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

access: Cemetery open to visitors (check maplegrovecemetery.org for hours)
transport: Kew Gardens station (E, F), about 0.8 km on foot
story: Jacob Riis planted these two beeches in 1905, beside the grave of his wife, Elizabeth. That is the whole of the record NYC Parks gives, and it is enough. Two American beeches, standing together at one grave in Maple Grove Cemetery in Kew Gardens, have been growing there for about 120 years, and since 1985 they have been on the city's list of Great Trees, entered as a pair. The planting date comes from that single Parks note. We know of no second source for it, so read 1905 as the city's word rather than a date carved anywhere. When Parks measured them in 1985, one trunk was 19 inches across and the other 26.4. The register gives a height of about 18.7 metres. Those measurements are forty years old now, and nobody has published newer ones, so if you bring a tape, tell us what you find. What these trees have witnessed is mostly the quiet business of a cemetery. More than a century of visitors walking between the stones, and a husband's memorial that kept growing long after the planting. A recent observation records the beeches still standing. The cemetery is open to visitors, but check maplegrovecemetery.org for hours before you go. Our pin is approximate, placed by the register inside the grounds, so look for the Riis grave and the two trunks beside it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a pair of American beeches standing together at one grave, the larger trunk about 26 inches across. They stand by the grave of Elizabeth Riis in Maple Grove Cemetery.
